problem: The units of R are inconsistent with the formula v ≈ R·E·t. If R is in volts per (W/m²) and E is in W/m², then R·E is in volts, and multiplying by t in seconds leaves an extra second — the equation would give volt-seconds, not volts.
fix: Define R as the responsivity in volts per unit radiant exposure, that is volts per (W·s/m²) or volts per (J/m²). Then v ≈ R·E·t is dimensionally correct: R (V·m²/J) × E (W/m²) × t (s) = volts.

problem: A flatbed scanner is listed as an application of the single-sensor arrangement. Flatbed scanners use a line sensor (a row of CCD or contact-image-sensor elements) swept across the page, not a single element. Drum scanners are the classic single-sensor example.
fix: Single sensor with a moving stage (drum scanners and laboratory stage scanners), line sensor with pushbroom motion (flatbed and document scanning, satellite scanning), and array sensor (phone and machine-vision cameras).

problem: Saying the ADC samples 'at fixed positions' blurs the two jobs. In an array camera the spatial sampling positions are fixed by the sensor element spacing, not chosen by the ADC; the ADC mainly quantizes the already-sampled element voltages.
fix: The digitizer does two jobs: sampling, fixing the positions (sensor element spacing) or instants at which the signal is read, and quantization, rounding each reading to the nearest of a fixed set of integers. In an array camera the element grid fixes the positions and the ADC quantizes.

problem: 1,024,000 bytes is not really 1 MiB (1 MiB = 1,048,576 bytes); it is 1.024 MB decimal and about 0.977 MiB. The chapter is careful about MB versus MiB elsewhere, so this slips.
fix: Bytes = 8,192,000 ÷ 8 = 1,024,000 bytes, that is 1.024 MB (about 0.977 MiB, roughly 1 MB). Time = 500 ÷ 250 = 2 s.
